records.sourceFile: The Infuence of Caffeine Supplementation on Resistance Exercise- A Review.pdf

paper.citation: Grgic J, Mikulic P, Schoenfeld BJ, Bishop DJ, Pedisic Z. The Influence of Caffeine Supplementation on Resistance Exercise: A Review. Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: A review that critically evaluates the evidence on caffeine supplementation before resistance exercise and gives practical guidelines on dosing. It covers maximal strength, muscular endurance, power, perceived exertion, pain, muscle damage, hormones, blood pressure, caffeine form, habitual intake, timing, genetics and placebo effects.
paper.tldr: Caffeine appears to acutely raise maximal strength, muscular endurance and power in resistance exercise, and doses of 3 to 9 mg per kg about 60 minutes before exercise look adequate. It can raise blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure need caution.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the caffeine and resistance exercise literature, covering 1RM, isometric and isokinetic strength, muscular endurance, power, delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle damage, hormonal and cardiovascular responses, dose, timing, caffeine form and genetics. The authors draw on earlier meta-analyses, and no systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors report that caffeine increases 1RM and MVC strength and muscular endurance, and enhances power, with effects that may depend on dose and external load. Effects on perceived exertion and pain perception are inconsistent, and there is preliminary evidence that caffeine can reduce soreness. Caffeine acutely increases systolic blood pressure in several studies, while the hormone increases are of questionable practical significance.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, and most of the underlying studies have small samples, are mostly in men, and often include untrained or recreationally trained participants. Placebo effects and blinding are a concern, and the authors call for research in women, competitive powerlifters and weightlifters, and long-term adaptation.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest starting with a lower dose such as 3 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before exercise, then adjusting to the individual. Athletes in power-dominated events may consider caffeine before training, and caution is advised for people with high blood pressure.
paper.athleteDev: For strength and power sessions, a pre-session caffeine dose of about 3 to 9 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before training may help, starting low and adjusting to the athlete's response. Evidence in trained athletes is thin because most studies used untrained or recreationally trained men.
paper.rtp: This review does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its blood pressure findings are relevant to health screening rather than rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: The Muscle Protein Synthetic Response to Meal Ingestion Following Resistance‑Type Exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Trommelen J, Betz MW, van Loon LJC. The Muscle Protein Synthetic Response to Meal Ingestion Following Resistance-Type Exercise. Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: A review of dietary and non-dietary factors that modify the muscle protein synthetic response to feeding after resistance-type exercise. It covers protein amount, protein type, digestion and absorption rate, mixed-meal composition, micronutrients, alcohol, habitual energy and protein intake, exercise, ageing, sex, body size and whole-body protein balance.
paper.tldr: About 20 g of rapidly digestible protein gives a near-maximal muscle protein synthesis response after resistance exercise, and 40 g or more may suit slower proteins or long gaps between meals. Alcohol and prolonged energy restriction can blunt the response.
paper.methods: Narrative review by the authors of studies on protein dose, protein type, digestion kinetics, mixed meals, micronutrients, alcohol, habitual intake, exercise, ageing, sex, body size and whole-body protein balance. No search method is described.
paper.findings: Around 20 g of isolated, rapidly digestible protein gives a near-maximal response at rest and after exercise, and doubling to 40 g adds about 10 to 20%. Animal proteins generally produce more synthesis than plant proteins, and slower proteins may need 40 g or more for a prolonged response. Alcohol and prolonged energy restriction reduce the response, and a higher protein intake can offset some of the reduction during energy restriction; findings on excess body fat are inconsistent and likely confounded by activity level.
paper.limitations: Most evidence comes from isolated protein drinks given over 4 to 5 hours, mostly in healthy young adults, so transfer to mixed meals, longer periods and older athletes is uncertain. Only one study has measured muscle protein synthesis after a mixed meal, and synthesis is a short-term marker that does not always match changes in muscle mass.
paper.practicalImplications: A practical per-meal target after resistance exercise is about 20 g of high-quality, fast-digesting protein. Slower proteins or long gaps before the next meal may call for 40 g or more, and the authors suggest older athletes aim for about 30 g per meal. Binge drinking and high-dose antioxidant supplements should be avoided around training.
paper.athleteDev: After resistance sessions, about 20 g of high-quality protein gives a near-maximal response, and slower proteins such as casein may need 40 g or more if the next meal is six or more hours away. Limit binge drinking around training, because alcohol blunts the response to protein.
paper.rtp: This review concerns healthy, mainly young adults after resistance exercise and does not study injured athletes or return to sport. The authors note that disuse and lower intake can reduce the protein response, but this was not tested in injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans.pdf

paper.citation: Trommelen J, van Lieshout GAA, Nyakayiru J, Holwerda AM, Smeets JSJ, Hendriks FK, et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4:101324.
paper.abstract: Randomized, placebo-controlled tracer study in 36 healthy, recreationally active young men who ingested 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a single bout of resistance exercise. The authors report that the magnitude and duration of the postprandial anabolic response, including plasma amino acid availability, muscle protein synthesis and whole-body protein balance, increased with the larger dose, while protein oxidation was barely affected.
paper.tldr: A single 100 g protein dose after resistance exercise produced a larger and longer-lasting muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g in healthy young men. The study does not show that larger doses improve training outcomes, and it did not test athletes.
paper.methods: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in healthy, recreationally active men aged 18 to 40, with 12 per group ingesting 0, 25 or 100 g of intrinsically labelled milk protein after a whole-body resistance exercise session. A quadruple isotope tracer feeding-infusion approach with plasma and muscle biopsies was sampled over 12 hours to measure amino acid kinetics, whole-body protein synthesis and oxidation, and muscle protein synthesis.
paper.findings: Plasma amino acid availability and tracer incorporation into muscle were higher after 100 g than 25 g over the 12-hour period. Myofibrillar protein synthesis (the primary outcome, based on the plasma leucine precursor) differed between all three doses, and was about 20% higher with 100 g than 25 g in the first 4 hours and about 40% higher from 4 to 12 hours. Whole-body protein synthesis increased with both protein doses, while the rise in amino acid oxidation was negligible in comparison.
paper.limitations: The sample was 12 healthy, recreationally active men per group, tested after a single session, so the findings may not extend to trained athletes, women, older adults or clinical groups. Several responses had not returned to baseline by 12 hours, and tracer recycling means the rates are likely underestimates, so the authors describe their 100 g estimates as minimal. The title's claim of no upper limit rests on testing only three doses within one 12-hour window.
paper.practicalImplications: A single 100 g protein dose gave a greater and longer muscle protein synthesis response than 25 g after resistance exercise in healthy young men, so the 20 to 25 g per meal guidance may not cap the acute response. The study does not show that such doses are needed, practical or better for athletes, or that meal size changes training gains.
paper.athleteDev: The study measured acute protein synthesis after one session, not strength, muscle mass or performance gains, so it cannot show that larger post-training protein doses improve adaptation. It is best used to inform recovery nutrition discussions about meal protein size, pending evidence from trained athletes.
paper.rtp: Participants were healthy, recreationally active men with no injury, so the study cannot inform nutrition for recovery from injury or return to sport. The authors note that clinically compromised or less active people may respond differently, which would also apply to injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The benefits of Vitamin D supplementation for athletes - Better performance and reduced risk of COVID-19.pdf

paper.citation: Grant WB, Lahore H, Rockwell MS. The Benefits of Vitamin D Supplementation for Athletes: Better Performance and Reduced Risk of COVID-19. Nutrients. 2020;12:3741.
paper.abstract: This narrative review proposes that vitamin D supplementation could improve athletic performance and reduce the risk and severity of COVID-19 in athletes. It summarises observational COVID-19 studies, early vitamin D treatment trials, proposed mechanisms, and studies of vitamin D in athletes. The authors conclude that athletes should consider supplementation as an additional means of reducing COVID-19 risk, alongside official guidelines.
paper.tldr: A narrative review argues that vitamin D could help athletes perform better and lower their COVID-19 risk, but most of the evidence is observational or from very small trials. Treat it as a hypothesis to check with a blood test and medical advice, not as proof that supplements protect athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The text gives no search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal. The authors draw on observational COVID-19 studies, two small treatment trials, mechanistic studies, and small studies in athletes and other adults, which are summarised in Tables 1 and 2.
paper.findings: The review cites more than 15 observational studies in which lower 25(OH)D went with greater COVID-19 risk or severity, although three reported no benefit; one Chicago cohort of 489 patients gave a relative risk of 1.77 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.81) for vitamin D deficiency. Two small treatment trials are described: a calcifediol trial (50 treated, 26 controls) with one ICU admission among treated patients and 13 among controls, and a vitamin D3 trial (16 treated, 24 controls) in which 63% and 22% respectively became SARS-CoV-2 RNA negative. In athletes, the review tabulates a 12-week trial of 19 college swimmers given 5000 IU/day, whose 25(OH)D rose from 47 to 61 ng/mL and who did better on deadlift and vertical jump than controls, and a winter supplementation study of 118 NCAA Division I athletes in which the stress fracture rate fell from 7.5% to 1.7%. The review's own table also lists a meta-analysis of 163 healthy athletes given 5000 IU/day that found no significant effect on muscle strength, and the muscle-recovery trials it cites were in recreationally or modestly active adults, not athletes.
paper.limitations: The review states no search or quality appraisal, so its choice of studies cannot be checked. The COVID-19 treatment trials are very small, and most athlete studies are small and short, with several observational. Two of three authors declare funding from Bio-Tech Pharmacal, Inc., and the 40 ng/mL target and 4000 to 10,000 IU/day dose are the authors' own advice, not outcomes tested in these studies. The abstract cites about 30 observational COVID-19 studies while the body text describes more than 15, and the COVID-19 trials were in hospitalised patients rather than athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Measure 25(OH)D in athletes at higher risk of low status, such as athletes with darker skin, who had lower 25(OH)D in the review's data, and discuss any supplementation with a physician or dietitian. The review's dosing advice rests on the authors' extrapolation, so it should not be applied as a standard protocol, and athletes should keep following official COVID-19 guidance on masks, distancing and testing.
paper.athleteDev: Use 25(OH)D testing to identify athletes with low status. The performance evidence is mixed: one meta-analysis of 163 athletes found no significant strength effect, and the recovery benefits come from small trials in non-athlete adults, so gains for athletes with adequate levels are unclear.
paper.rtp: The review addresses vitamin D, COVID-19 and general athletic performance, and it does not study return to sport after injury or illness. It recommends physician monitoring before athletes return after COVID-19 but gives no return-to-play protocol, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete.

records.sourceFile: The birth of modern sports nutrition  tracing the path from muscle biopsies to creatine supplementation A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Stout JR, Kreider RB, Candow DG, Forbes SC, Rawson ES, Antonio B, et al. The birth of modern sports nutrition: tracing the path from muscle biopsies to creatine supplementation-A narrative review. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2025;22(sup1):2463373.
paper.abstract: This narrative review traces sports nutrition research from the 1960s to the early 1990s at the Metabolic Research Laboratory in Stockholm. It covers muscle biopsy techniques, the links between muscle glycogen, diet and exercise, and the 1992 demonstration that oral creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine. The authors conclude that these laboratory discoveries shaped current performance and clinical applications of sports nutrition.
paper.tldr: A historical review traces how 1960s muscle biopsy work led to the rediscovery of creatine monohydrate in 1992. It explains where sports nutrition ideas came from, but it is not a systematic evidence review and several authors have industry ties.
paper.methods: Narrative review that combines personal accounts, including first-hand perspectives from Roger Harris (the acknowledgments also credit Kent Sahlin for input), with seminal studies from the Metabolic Research Laboratory. The text describes no search strategy, selection criteria or quality appraisal, and the review states that it is not a comprehensive examination of sports nutrition research.
paper.findings: Bergstrom and Hultman's 1966 biopsy study found that muscle glycogen fell in the exercised leg and rose to 50-60% above the rested leg after three days of high-carbohydrate diet. The 1967 study showed that starting glycogen level was closely related to endurance exercise duration. In the 1992 human study of 17 people aged 20-62 years, repeated 5 g creatine monohydrate doses over 4.5 to 21 days raised mean total creatine from 126.8 to 148.6 mmol/kg dry muscle, with the largest rises in people with the lowest starting levels, and no adverse effects were reported.
paper.limitations: The text does not describe a placebo group for the 1992 study, and the review does not report sport performance outcomes from it, although the abstract says creatine significantly improved exercise performance. The review also notes that a 50 g per day trial in horses showed no change in muscle creatine, and that the early 1975 pilot in two swimmers was wrongly judged negative. The authors' disclosure lists industry grants, consulting, sponsored research and advisory roles, and the review was unfunded.
paper.practicalImplications: The review supports the view that oral creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine, and that high-carbohydrate intake raises muscle glycogen, which are the mechanisms behind two common practices. Because the review is historical and industry-linked, check current trials for the specific sport, dose and athlete group before recommending either practice.
paper.athleteDev: Use the review as background for why carbohydrate loading (glycogen) and creatine loading (muscle creatine) are used. Confirm current evidence for any performance claim before building it into a programme, since the 1992 result reported in the text is a muscle measure, not a sport outcome.
paper.rtp: This review is a historical account of muscle metabolism and supplement research in people and horses. It does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions or supplement use during rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: The effect of pre-exercise hyperhydration on exercise performance, physiological outcomes and gastrointestinal symptoms - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Jardine WT, Aisbett B, Kelly MK, Burke LM, Ross ML, Condo D, et al. The Effect of Pre-Exercise Hyperhydration on Exercise Performance, Physiological Outcomes and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: Pre-exercise hyperhydration with osmotic aids is proposed to offset dehydration and heat stress during prolonged exercise in the heat. The authors searched three databases for English full-text studies comparing hyperhydration with a baseline or placebo condition, and rated study quality with the American Dietetic Association checklist. Thirty-eight studies were included. Hyperhydration may improve capacity during constant work rate exercise, which the authors attribute to lower heart rate and core temperature alongside higher plasma volume, and gastrointestinal symptoms varied across studies.
paper.tldr: Pre-exercise hyperhydration may help capacity in constant-pace exercise in the heat, possibly by lowering heart rate and core temperature. The evidence is mostly from male participants, and gut symptoms vary widely.
paper.methods: Systematic review of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase (final search 11 October 2022) for English full-text studies comparing a hyperhydration intervention with baseline or placebo. Exercise studies had to involve at least recreational athletes (training at least three times and 5 h per week). Study quality was assessed with the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria Checklist, with two authors screening and rating quality.
paper.findings: Of 38 studies (403 participants, 361 male), 22 assessed performance or capacity. Two studies reported time-trial improvements (5.7-11.4%), three reported more work completed (4-5%), and five of seven time-to-exhaustion studies reported higher exercise capacity (14.3-26.2%). Nine studies reported lower mean heart rate during constant work rate exercise, eight reported lower mean core temperature, and ten reported higher plasma volume. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26 studies.
paper.limitations: Most participants were male, and only one study included females only, with none adequately accounting for menstrual cycle phase. Few studies examined endurance running or field settings, and the capacity gains come from time-to-exhaustion tests, which the authors note are less reliable than time-trials. Gastrointestinal symptoms were not assessed with validated, reliable tools.
paper.practicalImplications: In hot conditions, a hyperhydration protocol may help steady-pace endurance work, with lower heart rate and core temperature reported in several studies, but performance gains are reported in only a few studies. The review notes that splitting the dose into smaller aliquots did not increase gut symptoms, and symptoms may vary with product, dose and ingestion rate.
paper.athleteDev: For endurance performance staff, the review supports testing pre-exercise hyperhydration as a heat strategy for constant-pace efforts, with attention to fluid retention and gut comfort. Expect the clearest effects on heart rate and core temperature rather than guaranteed time-trial gains.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review covers healthy athletes in performance trials in the heat and does not address injury, rehabilitation or clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: The impact of dietary factors on the sleep of athletically trained populations - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Barnard J, Roberts S, Lastella M, Aisbett B, Condo D. The Impact of Dietary Factors on the Sleep of Athletically Trained Populations: A Systematic Review. Nutrients. 2022;14:3271.
paper.abstract: A systematic review of 35 studies that examined dietary factors and sleep or sleepiness in athletically trained people, 21 of them rated positive quality. Evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg was associated with poorer sleep, while the protein and carbohydrate findings were mixed.
paper.tldr: Late-day caffeine, especially above about 2 mg/kg, was the clearest dietary factor linked to poorer sleep in trained athletes. Carbohydrate and protein timing findings are mixed, and the probiotic and beetroot evidence rests on few small trials.
paper.methods: A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021264200) of four databases from inception to May 2022, with title and abstract screening by one reviewer, full-text review by two, and quality rating with the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist. Included studies had trained or athletic adults, a dietary factor and a sleep or sleepiness outcome.
paper.findings: Evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg reduced sleep duration and sleep efficiency and increased sleep latency and wake after sleep onset in several studies. A high-GI meal after evening exercise improved polysomnography sleep in one study of recreationally trained men, but a basketball study showed no effect, and most tryptophan-rich protein trials showed no change. Probiotic and beetroot findings came from few small studies.
paper.limitations: Only 61% of studies were randomized trials, and females made up 26% (82 of 314) of randomized trial participants in the results, which the limitations section rounds to 20%, so causality and generalization are limited. The abstract's claim about tryptophan-rich protein is stronger than the body-text results, where three of four studies found no sleep change.
paper.practicalImplications: Screen athletes who report poor sleep for late-day caffeine and trial earlier or lower-dose intake, since evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg was consistently linked to worse sleep. A high-GI carbohydrate meal after evening exercise is a reasonable individual test, since one study found better sleep after it.
paper.athleteDev: The most actionable point for performance staff is timing: evening caffeine above about 2 mg/kg before training or competition was linked to shorter, less efficient sleep, so screen and adjust caffeine use around evening sessions.
paper.rtp: This review does not inform return to sport, because it included only healthy, non-injured athletes and studied sleep outcomes, not recovery from injury.
